n: After Ahab’s death, Moab—a kingdom east of the Dead Sea that Omri had conquered—breaks free. The Moabite Stone, an inscription by King Mesha, tells this same story from Moab’s side.
King Ahaziah falls through a latticed window or railing on his upper floor and is badly hurt. Instead of turning to the Lord, he sends to the Philistine god of Ekron to ask whether he will recover.

f.g: a wooden grille on a window or rooftop railing.
‘lord of flies,’ probably a mocking alteration of Baal-zebul, ‘Baal the prince.’
one of the five main Philistine cities.

n: The Lord sends Elijah to intercept the messengers with a pointed question: Is there no God in Israel, that you go to a foreign idol?
The answer to the king’s question comes from the true God, not Baal-zebub: he will never leave his bed.
The messengers return early, and the king asks why.
They repeat the stranger’s words exactly.
The king asks what the man looked like.

f.g: what kind of man; what did he look like?

n: Their description—a hairy man (or a man in a hairy cloak) with a leather belt—is instantly recognizable. John the Baptist, who came “in the spirit and power of Elias,” dressed the same way.

f.g: possibly ‘a man wearing a garment of hair.’

f.w: girt with a girdle of leather

n: The king sends a captain with fifty soldiers to arrest Elijah, who sits on a hilltop. The captain orders, “Man of God, the king says come down!”—treating God’s prophet as the king’s subject.

f.g: an officer commanding a unit of fifty soldiers.

n: Elijah answers with wordplay: if he truly is a “man of God,” let fire come down. Fire falls and consumes the captain and his men—showing who really holds power.

f.w: let fire come down from heaven

n: A second captain comes with fifty more and is even more demanding: “Come down quickly!”
Fire falls again and consumes them.
The third captain kneels and humbly pleads for his life and the lives of his men. Humility changes the outcome.
He acknowledges what happened to the others and asks for mercy.
The angel tells Elijah it is safe to go. Elijah comes down willingly to deliver God’s message in person.
Elijah repeats the sentence face to face: because the king sought Baal-zebub, he will die.
Ahaziah dies as foretold. Since he had no son, his brother Jehoram (also called Joram) becomes king of Israel. Confusingly, Judah’s king at the same time was also named Jehoram.

f.g: ‘Jehovah is exalted’; also spelled Joram. Two kings with this name ruled at the same time in Israel and Judah.

n: Ahaziah’s reign was brief and is recorded in Israel’s royal annals.
